extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and early-career creative writers submitting to literary magazines, residencies, fellowships, and agents
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and mindset advice for writers about submitting work to literary journals, residencies, fellowships, and agents—emphasizing submission strategy, persistence, and reframing rejection. Focuses on habits that increase acceptance chances and sustain creative practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect rejections / Set rejection goals
rubrics_metrics.description: “Collect rejections. Set rejection goals. I know someone who shoots for one hundred rejections in a year...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make rejection a quantitative, attainable target (e.g., 100 rejections/year) to reframe submitting as productive work rather than a sequence of failures. A goal to accumulate rejections encourages more submissions, increases chances of acceptances, and reduces the ego-sting of each individual denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize quantity over perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: From Art & Fear: students graded on quantity produced better work than those graded on a single perfect piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produce many pieces rather than obsessing over perfecting a few. Regular practice and iterative mistakes (high output) build skill and yield higher-quality work over time. Avoid paralysis by perfectionism; favor production and learning through making and revising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncouple rejection from failure / change your internal narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Reframe rejection so it is not synonymous with failure—'uncoupling the word "rejection" from "failure"' and 'turn down KFKD, or better yet, change the channel.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage the internal critic (Lamott's KFKD metaphor). View rejections as events in a process, not verdicts on your worth. Adopting this mindset reduces fear, preserves creative energy, and makes submitting sustainable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submit widely and persistently (batch your submissions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Launch determined 'air raids of submission grenades,' submitting five or ten pieces at a time and lining up the next tier of journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit multiple pieces simultaneously to a range of outlets (tiers). When rejected, immediately submit elsewhere rather than waiting. Batch submissions increase throughput and the statistical chance of acceptance while maintaining momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value encouraging rejections as meaningful signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Encouraging rejections (e.g., 'We liked this—try us again') are almost better for the soul than acceptances and can be invitations to submit again.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay attention to personalized or encouraging rejection notes from editors: they indicate interest or fit and can point to future opportunities. Treat these responses as constructive signals rather than mere rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take risks—don't let pursuit of acceptances make you timid
rubrics_metrics.description: If you had gone into last year shooting for five acceptances, it would have felt way too ambitious; aiming for rejections lets you take chances on big-name journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aiming for rejection lowers the emotional cost of aiming high. Submit to competitive/top-tier journals and prestigious opportunities because you have 'nothing to lose'; being risk-averse curtails growth and opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain intrinsic motivation—write for joy, not only for being read
rubrics_metrics.description: Submissions are not required to be a writer; some writers create joyfully without desire for publication—be happiest when writing, not when being read.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the practice of writing grounded in intrinsic rewards (the act of creation). Balance submission strategy with the personal, non-public reasons you write so that rejections don't undermine your creative life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat submissions as part of a career-long conversation and development
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeing rejection as a conversation: for every piece rejected, at least one other person read it, thought about it, and considered whether it would be a good fit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand submissions as interactions with editors and the literary community that advance your craft and career (revisions, residencies, networking). Rejections often lead to other opportunities (residencies, readings, future acceptances) and are part of professional development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn by reading and editorial work (use slush piles as education)
rubrics_metrics.description: Working as a reader/nonfiction editor is 'post-graduate education' in how not to start or what grips an editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage with submissions from the other side—read slush piles, volunteer, or study accepted/declined work—to learn effective openings, structure, and what editors respond to. That knowledge improves submission materials and craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical artifacts of rejection as motivators or talismans
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: King impaled rejection slips on a nail; the author saved slips in a box and shellacked a desk with them—turning rejection into ritualized evidence of effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting and displaying rejection slips or notes transforms them into symbols of persistence and progress. Ritualizing rejection (keeping slips, marking them) can sustain morale and remind you of continual effort toward eventual successes.
